summary: This section explains how a company passes ordinary and special resolutions. An ordinary resolution needs more votes in favour than against it. A special resolution needs votes in favour to be at least three times the number of votes cast against it.
points: An ordinary resolution requires proper notice to be given.
An ordinary resolution passes when votes in favour are more than votes against.
A special resolution requires the notice to specifically state the intention to propose it as a special resolution.
A special resolution requires votes in favour to be at least three times the votes cast against.
example: At Meera Textiles Private Limited, members gather for a general meeting after receiving proper notice. For a routine matter, 60 members vote in favour and 40 vote against, so the ordinary resolution passes because the yes votes exceed the no votes. Later, for a major change, the notice clearly states it is a special resolution. Here, 90 members vote in favour and 25 vote against. Because 90 is at least three times 25, the special resolution also passes successfully.

terms.meaning: A formal decision or proposal agreed upon by members of a company.
A person authorized by a member to attend and vote at a meeting on their behalf.
Voting by post or electronic means rather than attending the meeting in person.
A method of voting where votes are counted based on shares held rather than a simple show of hands.

watch: Remember that a special resolution requires three times the votes cast against it, not three times the total number of members.
